newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania cen.bank offers support to new government.
newsitem.headline: Romania cen.bank offers support to new government.

text.p: Romania's central bank (BNR) will support the incoming government in urgent measures to tackle the country's economic woes, governor Mugur Isarescu was quoted saying by independent news agency Mediafax on Monday.
"There is at this moment a window of opportunity to promote such (reform) policies," Isarescu told Mediafax.

Romania's centrist Democratic Convention (CDR) won parliamentary elections two weeks ago, ousting ruling leftists from seven years in power, and is to form a coalition with the Social Democrats (USD) of the former premier Petre Roman.

The reformists' triumph was consolidated by the victory of CDR leader Emil Constantinescu in Sunday's presidential election, with exit polls placing Constantinescu a comfortable seven points ahead of his rival Ion Iliescu.
Constantinescu has promised to implement reforms which stalled under ex-communist Iliescu's seven year rule.

Two weeks ago the CDR and USD signed a pact pledging to blend reforms -- including faster privatisation, liberalisation of currency markets and tough financial and monetary moves -- with promises of higher pensions, child benefits, soft credits for farmers housing and social welfare.
The BNR envisages combining monetary policy instruments, including the exchange rate, minimum reserve reqirements and interest rates, with fiscal policy to achieve economic stability, Mediafax said.

Analysts warn the new cabinet may have to give up costly social promises to remedy economic inbalances as inflation has rebounded above 45 percent, the leu currency had plunged and trade and budget deficit have risen.

They say a key issue in implementing the tough measures will be whether the central bank uses its tough won foreign exchange reserves to help stablise the local currency and fund winter energy imports.

The BNR, whose overall forex reserves stood at $1.0 billion at end-October, has recently begun to tighten its monetary policy, raising interest rates for its one-week refinancing funds to 51 percent from 49 percent.
Romania must also restore links with the International Monetary Fund, which, discontented with the pace of reforms, suspended loan tranches for the Balkan country this year.

The leu's retail rate sank to a street value of 5,100 to the dollar on Friday, a 44 percent depreciation in a month, before a rebound towards 4,600/4,900 on Monday. Officially it stands at an overvalued 3,495/3,515.
